Good question — the hard-margin SVM idea is best understood geometrically and in terms of robustness.

High-level idea
- A hard-margin SVM seeks a linear boundary (a hyperplane) that separates two classes with zero training errors, and among all such separating hyperplanes it picks the one that keeps the two classes as far apart as possible.  
- “As far apart as possible” means maximizing the gap (margin) between the classes; the boundary is placed midway between the nearest points from each class. Those nearest points are called support vectors — they determine the position of the hyperplane.

Why that is useful
- Maximizing the margin tends to improve generalization: a larger margin means small perturbations of inputs are less likely to change the predicted class.  
- The optimization problem is convex, so the solver finds a unique global solution when the data are strictly separable.

Key assumptions and limitations
- Hard-margin SVM requires the training data to be linearly separable. If they are not, there is no feasible solution.  
- It is sensitive to outliers: a single mismeasured point can force the margin to shrink dramatically or make separation impossible. That’s why practitioners often prefer soft-margin SVMs, which allow some misclassification in exchange for better robustness.
